Submission: month, DD, YYYY

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet covers Matthew Hopwood's contribution to team HaMaLoYa's project. The project is a drowsy-driver detection device and the subsystem covered in this datasheet is the board that controls a haptic motor in order to keep drivers awake.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: The goal of this project is to combine 4 separate subsystems together in order to create a system that accurately detects drowsiness and then acts to wake up drivers. The subsystem in this datasheet will be working to keep the driver awake by providing haptic alerts to the driver. It does this by connecting to the gyroscope board which lets this board know to when the driver is in a drowsy state. The haptic feedback stops when the device detects that the driver is no longer drowsy. Additional information about the system as a whole and the other specific subsystems can be found at the link here.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
Voltage Regulators

  1. L805CV Linear Regulator

    • $1/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Cheap and available Bad efficiency roughly 40% loss Up to 35V of input voltage Voltage tolerance not as good as other l7805 unit

  2. L7805ABV Linear Regulator

    • $1/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Cheap and available Bad efficiency roughly 40% loss Tighter tolerances on voltage output compared to the other L7805 Ever so slightly more expensive than the others

  3. MC7805CTG Linear Regulator

    • $1/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Cheap and available Bad efficiency roughly 40% loss Easy to model package and standard pin configuration for a breadboard Lower current output compared to the others at 1A

Choice: Option 2: L805CV Linear Regulator

Rationale: While its slightly more expensive than the others its basically negligible in regards to overall budget and its just a bit better than the others so its a worth it tradeoff.

H-Bridges

  1. Texas Instruments SN754410NE

    • $4.40/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Standard 16-DIP package for easy hand soldering or IC socket mounting. Bipolar transistor design creates ~1.2V–1.8V internal voltage drop, reducing voltage to the motor. Features built-in output ESD protection diodes. Max 1A continuous output current per channel.

  2. STMicroelectronics L298N

    • $13.60/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons High output current capacity (up to 2A continuous per channel). Large physical package with non-standard pin staggered row spacing. Accepts wide motor supply voltage ranges (up to 46V) High voltage drop requires external flyback diodes on custom PCBs.

  3. Texas Instruments L293D

    • $10.60/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Industry standard, extremely easy to find and drive with logic levels. Lower current handling capacity (600mA continuous per channel). Built-in internal clamp diodes protect against inductive kickback. High internal saturation voltage loss under heavy motor loads.

Choice: Option 1: Texas Instruments SN754410NE

Rationale: It is the most cost efficient option on top of checking all the necessary boxes and allowing for easy and effective design through its standard dip package.

Vibration Motors

  1. Vybronics VC1030B028F

    • $2.94/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Smallest footprint size compared to the others Weakest haptics of the bunch at 0.9G which may be too little Draws only ~64–80mA typical current Fixed single axis motion meaning vibration is restricted strictly perpendicular to the mounting plane.

  2. Vybronics VC1234B016F

    • $3.23/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Stronger haptics than the first option at 2G Larger footprint compared to the first one Deeper Vibration because it operates at a lower frequency Takes slightly longer to spin up to speed and stop due to its heavier internal rotating mass.

  3. Vybronics VZ7AL2B1692082

    • $4.04/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Significantly stronger than both options at 5.1G Cylindrical shape requires special housing/mounting compared to sticking it on part of the chasis Everything is fully enclosed so no need to worry about physical interference Largest by volume, while it is thinner it is taller

Choice: Option 3: Vybronics VZ7AL2B1692082

Rationale: They are are fairly similar in price and with that being taken into consideration the significantly improved haptics on option 3 make it the best fit. While the drawbacks in terms of size may require more design considerations the tradeoff of better haptics is well worth it.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The goal of the power budget is to get an idea of how much current will be flowing through all the devices in the subsystem. But also more importantly to confirm whether or not the component configuration will work properly and not over strain the voltage regulator. This was a concern as there is only one used voltage rail on the board which is 5V. That rail will power logic for the Nano and H-bridge while also powering the motor while other passive components take up power too. To be extra safe there is also a requirement for at least a 25% current safety margin on top of the base current usage.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: Using the calculations from the power budget we only use 110mA worth of current including the 25% extra safety margin. This is well within the output limit of the 5V regulator which can output 1A max.
